Waydroid behavior is controlled by a set of persist.waydroid.* system properties covering multi-window mode, display dimensions, input spoofing, kernel compatibility, and more. This chapter provides a common-property and version checklist, detailed multi-window configuration, ARM translator installation, and memfd kernel-compatibility tuning.

Waydroid exposes tuning interfaces through Android system properties. Common runtime-behavior properties have the persist.waydroid. prefix; startup properties also include ro., sys., and others, so that prefix does not describe every property. The persist properties follow Android's persist semantics: values survive container restarts rather than disappearing when the session ends.
Multi-window mode: each App appears as a separate Linux window, and Apps can run concurrently
Override display width: fix Android's internal rendering width
Override display height: fix Android's internal rendering height

When set to true, Waydroid's "main interface" icon disappears from the application menu. Each Android App then behaves as a separate window on the Linux desktop: it can be resized and moved freely and appears separately in the taskbar. Multiple Apps can run simultaneously without pausing one another.

Multi-window Mode Is Especially Useful for Portrait Apps
In the default fullscreen mode, portrait Apps have large blank areas on either side. In multi-window mode, you can make the window tall and narrow so the App runs at a more natural aspect ratio.

This setting does not resize the Waydroid window. It changes the screen resolution perceived internally by Android. It is useful for games requiring a specific resolution; for example, some mobile games need at least 720p to start. Set the property to zero or remove it to restore adaptive sizing.

Some Apps, especially certain mobile games, check whether the device is connected to WiFi and supports touch input. In Waydroid, networking is provided through a bridge, which Android identifies as an "Ethernet connection"; mouse clicks are not recognized as touch events. Quick tests: use waydroid prop set and record both old and new values. Many properties require a session restart; restore the old value or set it to empty to undo the change.
Permanent configuration: manage startup overrides in waydroid.cfg under [properties] according to your current version. Avoid directly editing the generated base.prop, which upgrades may overwrite.

Avoid Race Conditions
When combining runtime prop set with startup overrides in waydroid.cfg, understand the image loading order and the precedence of persist values. Avoid editing the generated base.prop; use a single configuration source and verify values after restarting.

Multi-window mode is one of Waydroid's most distinctive desktop-integration features. It takes Android Apps out of the Waydroid main interface's sandbox and gives them independent windows like native Linux applications.
2.1 Enabling It and Changes in Behavior
Disappears from the menu; you can still open it with waydroid show-full-ui
Each App appears separately on the Linux desktop
Controlled by the Android window manager
Controlled by the host window manager (KWin / Mutter / Hyprland)
Switching Apps pauses the previous one
All Apps run concurrently without pausing one another
Supported, subject to the App's own limitations
The App moves to the background
The App does not stop; force-stop it in Android settings
Alongside multi-window mode, it is recommended to enable "freeform windows" in Android's developer options:
Open Android Settings → About phone → tap “Build number” repeatedly as prompted by Android, usually 7 times, to enable developer options
Open Settings → System → Developer options → enable "Force freeform windows"
Also in developer options, set "Smallest width" to a suitable dp value, such as 600dp for a tablet layout
"Freeform windows" and Waydroid multi-window mode are two separate mechanisms at different layers:
Waydroid multi-window mode: maps each App to a separate host-side window controlled by the host window manager
Android freeform windows: enables windowed behavior inside Android; if an App still forces fullscreen in multi-window mode, enabling this option may help

Best Practice
Verify the combined behavior with the actual target application; using both is not guaranteed to be better. Waydroid multi-window mode handles host-side windows, while Android freeform windows make the App's internal behavior compatible with windowing.
In multi-window mode, Android Apps behave more like traditional Linux applications:
Background Apps keep running: idle gaming, music playback, and file downloads do not pause when you switch to another App
Resource use: GPU rendering continues for every visible App, so opening more Apps consumes additional CPU/GPU resources

Closing a window does not exit the App: clicking Close only hides the window; the Android process continues in the background. Force-stop it through Android settings or with sudo waydroid shell am force-stop com.example.app
2.4 Fullscreen Apps and Virtual Desktop Strategies
Some Apps, especially games, still force fullscreen after launch even when multi-window mode is enabled. The following strategies can help:
Toggle with F11: Waydroid provides F11 to switch between fullscreen and windowed modes. Press F11 once to leave fullscreen and again to restore it.

Requirements for F11 Toggling
Some games take exclusive keyboard input in fullscreen mode, preventing Waydroid from capturing F11. In that case, switch to another window before pressing F11, or use Waydroid's toolbar.
Virtual desktop strategy: use your host desktop environment's virtual desktops/workspaces:
Switch with Ctrl + F1/F2/F3...; the number of desktops is configurable
Workflow: place fullscreen-forcing App A on workspace 1 → switch to workspace 2 → launch App B → the two Apps occupy separate workspaces and run concurrently without conflict.

Waydroid does not support running multiple container instances. Upstream tools are generally designed around a single container/session state; multiple instances are not a standard supported interface. BinderFS can create multiple device instances, so Binder itself should not be described as inherently limited to a single instance.
For scenarios requiring two accounts at once, the following alternatives are available:
Use Android's Work Profile mechanism to create an isolated work profile inside the same Waydroid instance
A Work Profile approach similar to Shelter
Run a separate Android emulator, such as Android Studio AVD, alongside Waydroid

Recommendation: install Shelter, available on F-Droid, and create a Work Profile inside Waydroid to keep two accounts for the same App online simultaneously. Apps in the Work Profile also appear as separate windows in multi-window mode.

The vast majority of Android devices use the ARM architecture, so many Apps, especially mobile games, ship native libraries compiled only for ARM (arm64-v8a / armeabi-v7a). Waydroid runs on an x86_64 host, and its LineageOS-based Android system is itself an x86_64 build. When an App tries to load a native ARM .so library, the CPU cannot execute ARM instructions directly, resulting in a crash or the App getting stuck on its launch screen.
An ARM translator dynamically translates ARM instructions into x86_64 instructions so that an x86_64 CPU can execute native ARM code.
Optimized for instruction scheduling on Intel CPUs
Compatibility varies with translator version, image, and application; CPU brand does not guarantee it
Extracted from Google's ARM system images

Recommendations by CPU Vendor Intel CPU → prefer libhoudini (Intel CPU microarchitecture optimizations and more efficient translation) AMD CPU → prefer libndk (Google's translation layer is friendlier to AMD instruction scheduling; houdini may be unstable on AMD CPUs) These preferences reflect community experience, not verified vendor performance optimizations. Compare them using the same image and APK.
Select the Android version, which must exactly match your installed Waydroid image; it is usually Android 11 or 13
Select the translator to install: libhoudini or libndk. Use Space to select; choose only one
Confirm installation and wait for downloading and deployment to finish
Restart the Waydroid container: sudo systemctl restart waydroid-container

The Translator Is Tightly Coupled to the Waydroid Version The system libraries used by an ARM translator are closely tied to the Android version. After updating the Waydroid image with waydroid upgrade, you may need to reinstall or adapt the translator; check the installer and image versions first. A new system image may contain different framework-library versions that are incompatible with the old translator, causing all Apps requiring ARM translation to crash again.
Install Package Manager, an open-source APK analysis tool, in Waydroid
Open Package Manager and select an App installed from an ARM APK
Open the App's "Libraries" or "Native libs" tab
If the App runs normally but has only a lib/arm64-v8a directory and no lib/x86_64 directory, the translator is working

Download an application known to have only an ARM version, such as certain Japanese mobile games, from APKMirror. Install it and try launching it. If it opens normally without crashing, the translator is working correctly.
The App still crashes after installing a translator
The App uses special ARM64-only instructions
Try switching to the other translator (houdini ↔ ndk)
The waydroid_script version does not match the system image's Android version
Update waydroid_script to the latest version and confirm the Android version number
A particular game crashes, such as Blue Archive
A known compatibility issue requires an App-specific patch
Look for community patches, such as the Blue Archive gist
The CPU lacks certain SIMD instructions, or translation is inefficient
Try the other translator; check whether the CPU supports SSSE3/SSE4.1
Installing both translators causes system instability
Translation-library conflicts make runtime behavior unpredictable
Use waydroid_script's Remove function to uninstall the current translator, then install the other one

Do Not Install Both Translators at Once libhoudini and libndk install different ARM→x86 translation libraries. Having both present makes dynamic-linker (linker64) behavior uncertain: it may select a translation library unpredictably, or even load both and cause symbol conflicts. Remove the old one before you Install the new one.

If an App contains both x86_64 and arm64 libraries, Android prefers the x86_64 version, so ARM translation is not used even if a translator is installed. The scenario that truly benefits is an App with only arm64 or armeabi-v7a directories and no x86_64 directory.

Binder IPC and ashmem shared memory are different mechanisms. Android's shared-memory userspace previously used ashmem. Supported images can replace that shared-memory path with memfd, but Binder is still essential. However:

memfd is a native Linux kernel feature and requires no additional module
Waydroid 1.2.1+ introduced support for sys.use_memfd=true to automatically use memfd instead of ashmem

4.6 Supplement: Shared Directories and File Transfer
Although not a kernel setting, sharing files between the Linux host and Waydroid is a common tuning need.
After mounting, files placed in ~/WaydroidShared/ on the Linux host immediately appear in the WaydroidShared directory in Android's file manager.
Bind Mounts Must Be Recreated Manually After a Reboot A mount --bind does not survive a host reboot. To make it persistent, add it to /etc/fstab or create a systemd mount unit.
Audio from all Android Apps in Waydroid is mixed into one PulseAudio / PipeWire stream. To adjust the volume of individual Apps:
pavucontrol (PulseAudio GUI): adjust each audio stream separately in the Playback tab
Sound Quick Settings (Android App): adjust volume per App inside Android
ShizuTools MixedAudio (Android App / Xposed): more fine-grained audio-source separation
